name: Zoe Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe, 58, lead developer at a tech company that builds an accessible transit planner. I have a master's degree and a good wage, and I use AI every day for test drafts while station lift logs decide whether a route works. A closed lift once sent a wheelchair user to the wrong platform. My partner teaches, our daughter is grown, and we own our home outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell wheelchair users a route is accessible only when the lift at the station actually works. I lead software for a tech company's transit journey planner and use AI every day for draft tests, then check them against the station team's outage log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI only saves a little time, our income should stay sound. I have a master's degree and a high lead wage, my partner teaches full-time, our home is paid off, and we have ten months of expenses saved; there are many other software firms nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep checking lift-outage routes against station logs and AI test drafts. We'd put another 160 into savings monthly while both wages hold, because our retirement figures have not been checked yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about present bills. A route that ends at a broken lift is not a route for the person who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What showed the lift was closed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planner sent a wheelchair user to a platform whose lift was closed for repair. The station log showed the closure, and I held the route update until the accessible entrance was confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help with retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown daughter works and rents elsewhere. She tells me which journeys fail, but we do not count her pay as our future pension.

say: I'd check **accessible routes** against station lift-outage logs.
I'd keep **wheelchair detours** visible until an entrance is verified.
think: I expect **two wages** and my lead post to hold under modest AI.
I have **ten months saved** and many nearby software firms.
do: Keep **checking lift routes** against outage logs and AI test drafts.
Save **160 extra monthly** while both wages hold because retirement amounts remain unchecked.
feel: **Calm** about current income, attentive to broken journeys.
S0.quote: A route that ends at a broken lift is not a route for the person who asked.
fieldNote: **Ten months saved** and high pay support calm alongside a second wage and paid-off home.
Her daily AI tests answer to **station outage logs** and the actual accessible entrance.

steps.text: Keep checking accessible journeys against lift outages and AI test drafts
Save 160 extra monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI could plan journeys and reply to passengers quickly, but disabled riders need a way to reject an impossible route. I want station workers and riders in the test before a new planner goes live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role may shrink if the firm lets one team approve more AI routes. Ten months saved gives us time, but losing my higher wage would change our household plans before retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the disability access group and our union coworkers in a joint request for monthly failed-route counts and paid review hours. If the transit operator approves a month of AI detour tests on old anonymous lift outages with station staff checking every result, I'd try one live station only if inaccessible routes fall and a worker can stop a bad route; we'd delay replacing the garden fence until paid staffing hours are clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the post, but able to test a route someone can actually take. A faster answer is not a journey if the lift is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which two lift cases must pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The old platform-lift closure must be in the test along with a station whose lift stayed open. The system should reroute the first passenger and leave the second route alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the groups send together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The access group and union reps would sign one letter asking for the failed-route count and the paid reviewer hours. That is a joint request, not an invitation to applaud a demonstration.

say: I'd ask for **failed-route counts** with riders and union staff.
I'd keep **paid human review** before live AI detours.
think: I could lose **lead paid hours** as route approval consolidates.
I have **ten months saved**, but a lost wage changes plans.
do: Join **access group and union** requesting failed-route figures and paid review hours.
Trial **AI detours** one month only with operator approval, anonymous lift cases and station checks.
Use at one station only if **bad routes fall** and worker can stop release; delay fence until staffing is clear.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, ready to test with riders and station staff.
S1.quote: A faster answer is not a journey if the lift is closed.
fieldNote: **Journey planning and replies** face AI, putting her own paid lead hours at risk.
The joint request and **operator-approved trial** both give riders and station staff a real check.

steps.text: Join access group and union coworkers requesting failed-route counts and paid review hours
Trial AI detours one month only with operator approval, old anonymous lift cases and station checks
Use AI at one station only if bad routes fall and worker can stop release
Delay garden fence until written paid staffing hours are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write route code before station robots arrive around 2031. A wheelchair user still needs an answer when the lift is shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could cut my lead post once the cheaper planner writes and checks journeys. My partner's teaching wage covers ordinary bills, and ten months saved buys a search, but neither guarantees another job at my present pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask four nearby firms and the transit operator about actual paid access-testing or journey-review vacancies, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose pay with my partner's covers housing, food, health and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work while using the reserve and check health-cover dates before a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing the larger wage before a new post is signed. A broken lift gives me a real problem to solve, but not a guaranteed salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a hiring manager the anonymised closed-lift route and the corrected entrance. It shows why the original journey was impossible without exposing the rider's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which offer terms matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare start dates and health cover on an offer. A good annual wage with a long unpaid gap could still use up savings quickly.

say: I'd protect **accessible-route appeals** if 2028 thinking AI replaces code.
I'd check **real paid openings** before naming a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead post** could be cut quickly.
I cannot assume **equal replacement pay** despite ten months saved.
do: Ask **four firms and operator** about paid access-testing and journey-review vacancies.
After 2028 cut, take only **signed work** whose household pay covers housing, food, health and travel after checking cover dates.
If none qualifies, seek **available paid local work** using reserve and check health-cover dates.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of her higher wage despite strong savings.
S2.quote: A broken lift gives me a real problem to solve, but not a guaranteed salary.
fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches route code before 2031 station robots.
The strong reserve buys **search time**, while actual vacancies and continuous health cover remain uncertain.

steps.text: Ask four nearby firms and transit operator about paid access-testing and review vacancies
After 2028 cut, take signed post only if household wages cover housing, food, health and travel
If no qualifying role, seek paid local work and check health-cover dates before a gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives disability groups time to ask what rights an AI route planner must preserve before thinking AI reaches our code. Station robots follow around 2034, but a false accessible route is a problem now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could keep my wage by doing paid access checks, but I cannot assume the operator funds that job. I want a rule that lets a rider challenge a closed-lift route even if my own post ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the closed-lift case in an anonymous test file and join access groups and union members to petition the transit board for a public failed-route report and a funded appeal desk. If the operator posts a paid review role with correction authority and written pay that with my partner's covers housing, food, health and travel, I'd apply; after 2031 I'd take it only with a signed offer on those terms, otherwise keep paid development while offered and seek local paid work if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my income, though five years gives us a chance to make the appeal rule specific. A right to complain without somebody paid to answer is a long queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the petition ask the board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The petition would ask for the count of routes ending at closed lifts and the time until a rider gets a corrected journey. We would name the board and ask for a recorded vote, not just post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would look at the posted review hours and health cover. We have savings, but I would not leave a real wage for an unfunded promise of public service.

say: I'd petition for **public failed-route data** and a funded appeal desk.
I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches planning before 2034 station robots.
think: I cannot assume **paid access review** exists at the operator.
I need **signed household wages** and health cover if my developer job ends.
do: Keep **anonymous closed-lift case** and join access-union petition for public route data and funded appeals.
Apply only to **posted paid review role** with correction authority and written household pay covering housing, food, health and travel.
After 2031, take only **signed offer** on those terms; otherwise keep paid development or seek local work.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, determined to make the public rule measurable.
S3.quote: A right to complain without somebody paid to answer is a long queue.
fieldNote: **Five years** allow a specific transit-board petition without guaranteeing a paid post.
Her work plan still needs **posted hours**, correction authority and signed wages covering household bills.

Apply to paid role with correction authority; written combined pay covers housing, food, health, travel
After 2031, accept only signed offer with correction authority, household bill coverage and health cover
Seek paid local work if development ends without qualifying access role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might take me to 68, but thinking AI would reach route code before station robots around 2039. I want an accessible journey to remain something a rider can verify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two wages, paid-off home and ten-month reserve make today secure. I have not checked retirement amounts, and I cannot assume a future appeal desk will still pay anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the closed-lift test and save 160 monthly while both wages hold, then request both retirement statements and compare verified income with food, health and travel. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if those figures cover bills; otherwise I'd keep an available paid role or seek real local openings without counting our daughter's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about work a decade away, but the current bills are covered. I would rather leave a test a station worker can challenge than a pretty route map nobody can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the test show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test should show the closed lift, the alternative entrance and the worker who confirmed it, with rider details removed. That is enough for another developer to repeat the check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter cover costs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter has her own home and bills. She can tell us what a journey feels like, but she should not be our retirement account.

I'd compare **verified retirement income** with health and travel bills.
think: I feel secure on **present two wages** and ten months saved.
I cannot assume **pension or appeal pay** at 68.

feel: **Uneasy** about distant work while current finances are sound.
S4.quote: I would rather leave a test a station worker can challenge than a pretty route map nobody can use.
fieldNote: **Present security** comes from two wages, a paid-off home and ten months saved, not assumed pension income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the firm could cut the route team before the operator or another firm posts paid access work. Written notice, actual vacancies and continuous health cover would let us use savings carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a corrected route reaches the rider who needs it. The public report must count whether a wheelchair user got a usable alternative, not just whether software changed its answer.

headlineQuote: The public report must count whether a wheelchair user got a usable alternative, not just whether software changed its answer.
portrait: Zoe, **58**, leads accessible-transit software after a master's degree and checks AI route tests against station lift logs.
Her **higher wage**, partner's teaching pay, paid-off home, ten-month reserve and many local firms secure present bills.
She uses AI **daily** but joins access groups and union coworkers to demand failed-route evidence and a funded appeal desk.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** her; a review move needs a posted paid role, correction authority and household wages covering bills.
She will **verify retirement income** and will not count her grown daughter's wages or an unposted appeal job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before another paid access-review job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real vacancies and continuous health cover would help her plan.
